title: New Covenant
summary: Jeremiah 31 promises a covenant with Israel and Judah in which God’s instruction is written on the heart, knowledge of God is shared, and sin is forgiven. Ezekiel 36 adds cleansing, a new heart, and God’s Spirit. At the Last Supper, Jesus identifies the cup with the new covenant in his blood; Paul and Hebrews then interpret covenant ministry, mediation, sacrifice, and forgiveness in light of that promise. These passages share a covenant-renewal theme, while each contributes a different part of the picture.
historical_context: Jeremiah presents the promise within a sequence of restoration hopes for Israel and Judah; Ezekiel 36 likewise speaks of gathering and renewal. Luke places Jesus’ words over the cup at the meal before his death. Second Corinthians and Hebrews reflect on the new covenant in letters to their readers. These are the settings represented in the cited texts; no additional historical reconstruction is supplied by the object’s sources.
canonical_context: Jeremiah’s promise supplies language that Hebrews explicitly quotes and develops. Ezekiel also describes inward renewal and the Spirit; Luke connects the covenant with Jesus’ death; 2 Corinthians discusses ministry of the new covenant; and Hebrews relates its mediation to sacrifice and forgiveness. The passages form a clear canonical conversation, but their distinct wording and arguments should not be merged into a single undifferentiated claim.
literary_context: Jeremiah and Ezekiel announce restoration in prophetic speech. Luke embeds the covenant saying in the meal narrative. Paul’s letter reflects on ministry, while Hebrews quotes Jeremiah and builds an extended argument about covenant, mediation, and sacrifice. Noticing the quotation and each text’s literary purpose helps explain how the later passages receive the earlier promise.
covenantal_significance: The promise in Jeremiah addresses Israel and Judah and describes internalized instruction, shared knowledge of God, and forgiveness. Ezekiel adds cleansing and the Spirit. Jesus’ words over the cup connect covenant renewal with his death, and Hebrews interprets that connection through its account of mediation and sacrifice. The texts portray renewal as involving forgiveness and transformed allegiance, with different authors emphasizing different aspects.
canonical_role: The new-covenant theme links prophetic promises of restoration with New Testament accounts of Jesus’ death and later reflection on covenant ministry and mediation. Jeremiah’s wording is especially important because Hebrews quotes it directly; the other texts contribute related but distinct claims.

interpretive_notes.note: The new covenant fulfills the earlier covenants rather than erasing them.
Do not detach the new covenant from forgiveness, Spirit gift, and covenant obedience.

common_questions: How does the new covenant relate to the Old Testament?
Why does Jesus speak about a new covenant at the Last Supper?
